The MORCIC project aims to propose new MOR techniques that perform better than commercial tools like ANSYS RaptorX.

The conventional BT method involves the solution of computationally expensive Lyapunov equations and the application of singular value decomposition (SVD), which hinders its applicability to large-scale models.
The proposed low-rank BT MOR approach uses an efficient low-rank technique based on the extended Krylov subspace (EKS) to solve the Lyapunov equations.
The MORCIC tool was developed in C++ using the CMake automation software and evaluated on a Linux workstation with a 2.80 GHz 16-thread Intel® Xeon Silver 4309Y CPU and 64 GB of memory.
The small-scale RC and RLCk models used for the initial BT MOR evaluation had orders ranging from 48 to 21,800 nodes, 2 to 12,166 ports, and up to 23,639,237 mutual inductors.
The mean relative error (MRE) and maximum relative error (MAX RE) for the DC and S-parameter analyses of the initial BT MOR ROMs were below 0.73% and 1.89%, respectively.
The reduction in ROM order for the small-scale models ranged from 64.58% to 87.17%.
The large-scale RLCk models used for the low-rank BT MOR evaluation had orders ranging from 95,189 to 162,881 nodes, 4 to 13 ports, and up to 98,585,323 mutual inductors.
The low-rank BT MOR approach achieved a maximum reduction in ROM order of 5.5 times compared to the ROMs obtained by ANSYS RaptorX.
The accuracy of the MORCIC ROMs was comparable to the RaptorX ROMs, with the insertion loss error being lower than 0.5 dB and the phase differences being less than 2 degrees.
On average, the MORCIC tool produced ROMs that were 3.1 times more compact than the RaptorX ROMs.
The reduction time and memory requirements of the MORCIC tool were higher than RaptorX but still reasonable and can be improved in future work.
The benchmark circuits used for evaluation included Hybrid and Wilkinson couplers, VGAs, VCOs, and LNAs, covering a wide range of analog and mixed-signal circuits.
The key metrics used for evaluation included S-parameters, gain, linearity, noise performance, and other circuit-specific characteristics.
The proposed low-rank BT MOR approach can be integrated into industrial extraction tools like ANSYS RaptorX to obtain more compact ROMs of large-scale multi-port RLCk models.
